nameStory: Good King Henry gets its royal name from a case of mistaken identity! Originally called "Good Henry" in German to distinguish it from "Bad Henry" (a poisonous plant), English speakers later added "King" to the name, though no actual monarch was involved. In German folklore, Henry was a popular name for helpful garden spirits and household elves, making this the "good" spirit of the vegetable patch.
description: Good King Henry is a leafy perennial plant that looks like a robust, triangular-leaved spinach relative. This Old World vegetable stands about 1-3 feet tall with thick, fleshy stems and distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that have a slightly mealy texture. Though once a cottage garden staple, it's now extremely rare in New England, more likely encountered as an escaped garden relic than a wild plant. The plant produces small, inconspicuous greenish flowers in dense spikes during summer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive triangular to arrow-shaped leaves with smooth edges, often with a slightly silvery or mealy coating that feels dusty to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sturdy perennial that grows 1-3 feet tall with thick, somewhat succulent stems that feel substantial and fleshy when squeezed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers clustered in dense, leafless spikes that rise above the foliage, lacking any colorful petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are larger and more triangular, while upper leaves become narrower and more lance-shaped as they ascend the stem

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark seeds enclosed in papery coverings that remain on the dried flower spikes into fall

habitat: In New England, Good King Henry is most likely found near old homesteads, abandoned gardens, or disturbed areas where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers rich, fertile soils and can tolerate partial shade, often persisting for years after gardens have been abandoned. Look for it around old stone foundations, farmyards, or areas with deep, well-composted soil.

seasonality.spring: New triangular leaves emerge early from the perennial rootstock, appearing fresh and tender with a distinctive mealy coating. This is when the plant was traditionally harvested as "poor man's asparagus."
seasonality.summer: Dense spikes of tiny greenish flowers appear above the mature foliage, followed by small seed development. Leaves remain present but become tougher and less palatable.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes turn brown and papery while retaining seeds, and leaves begin to yellow and die back to the ground. Seeds may be dispersed by wind and wildlife.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground roots, leaving only dried stems and seed heads as evidence of its presence until spring regrowth.

funFact: Good King Henry was so valued as a vegetable that every part of the plant was eaten - young leaves as spinach, flower spikes as broccoli substitutes, and the tender spring shoots were blanched and served like asparagus, earning it the nickname "poor man's asparagus" among English cottage gardeners.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with lamb's quarters, but Good King Henry has more triangular, arrow-shaped leaves and grows as a perennial from the same root system year after year, while lamb's quarters has more diamond-shaped leaves and grows as an annual. Remember: "King Henry keeps his crown" - it's the perennial one that returns each spring.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this plant's "mercury" common names with the poisonous dog's mercury - they're in completely different plant families. The mercury names refer to the Roman god Mercury due to supposed medicinal properties, not the toxic metal. This edible plant was brought to New England by European colonists but never became widely established.
compareHints: Good King Henry is the only Blitum species commonly found in New England gardens or as an escape. It's most similar to other members of the amaranth family like lamb's quarters and orache, but differs by being perennial rather than annual, and having more consistently triangular leaves. Unlike its annual cousins, Good King Henry develops a substantial root system that allows it to return year after year from the same spot.
